material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Under the dossier contact scope, X0 should give the largest single-contact organic recovery and strongest product/impurity discrimination, although the dossier may be misindexed. A 0.03 L aqueous / 0.018 L organic contact should place about 41% of product in organic for a representative product-rich feed. Test: otherwise matched contacts should favor X0; contrary phase measurements or final assays would overturn this.

## H2 [tentative]
Reaction outcome likely depends categorically on catalyst/solvent and continuously on temperature and residence time. I will screen categories before refining conditions. A useful process must jointly meet final purity >=0.80 and maximize recovery, so selection will be based on final assays rather than native score alone.

## Decision plan
Use the 12 paid nonfinal observations chiefly as HPLC diagnostics, one per batch, while preserving all 12 final assays. Screen broad reaction conditions, then refine the best region and apply extraction/purification with X0 as the initial prior. Avoid treating anonymous indices as ordered variables.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [unresolved]
The dossier predicts X0 as the strongest organic extractor under its stated contact scope, but batch 1 did not satisfy purity and had effectively zero measured final recovery after extraction/wash/concentration (events runner-operation-0008 through -0016). This does not isolate extraction performance because the C0/S0 reaction itself had very low target yield; the apparent high final conversion in the retained organic phase is a phase-selection artifact rather than reaction conversion.

## H2 [supported only for short 350 K screen]
At 350 K and 1200 s, all screened C0/S0–S3 and C1–C3/S0 reactions had low conversion (~0.08–0.13 by final assay). C1/S0 gave the best selectivity/purity of this limited screen (~0.52), while C2/S0 was poorest (~0.20). Differences exceed the declared single-assay noise but lack replication; solvent–catalyst interactions remain unresolved (events runner-operation-0024, -0032, -0040, -0048, -0056, -0064).

## H3 [prospective]
Low conversion across categories suggests residence time/temperature, rather than category alone, is limiting. Next test: C1/S0 at 400 K for 7200 s should substantially raise conversion; excessive byproduct/degradation would instead favor a milder refinement. I will then test promising solvent interactions and reserve later batches for a complete separation process.

## Decision rule
Prioritize final purity >=0.80 first, then recovery. Do not use phase-specific conversion after separation as evidence of reaction completion.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [rejected for this process]
The dossier's X0 organic-extraction prior did not transfer reliably to the tested reaction mixtures. The optimized-feed separation in batch 12 changed a pre-extraction HPLC estimate of purity 0.578 and recovery 0.421 (runner-operation-0101) to final-assay purity 0.325 and recovery 0.038 (runner-operation-0111). Batch 1 also lost essentially all measurable recovery (runner-operation-0016). Phase-specific conversion near one after separation reflects depletion of reactant from the retained phase and is not reaction completion.

## H2 [supported in tested scope]
For C1 at 400 K and 7200 s, S2 was the best of S0–S3 without downstream separation: batch 10 achieved final purity 0.576, recovery 0.432, conversion 0.836, and score 0.387 (runner-operation-0088). S0 and S1 were numerically lower in recovery (0.335 and 0.369; runner-operation-0072 and -0080), while S3 was clearly poorer in purity/recovery (0.353/0.232; runner-operation-0096). These are single batches, so fine S0–S2 ranking is not replicated.

## H3 [supported]
Long/hot processing substantially improved conversion versus the 350 K, 1200 s screens: C1/S0 rose from about 0.084 conversion (runner-operation-0048) to 0.721 (runner-operation-0072), with broadly similar selectivity. Temperature and time are confounded, so their individual effects remain unresolved.

## Final decision
No completed batch met the required purity >=0.80. Batch 1 is selected as the closest approach to that hard constraint (purity 0.742, runner-operation-0016), while explicitly recognizing its measured recovery was zero and thus it is not a successful feasible process. Batch 10 is the recovery-leading fallback but fails the purity threshold more severely. A future campaign should screen actual extractant identity/retained phase and wash intensity on the C1/S2 long-reaction feed before repeating reaction optimization.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–workup system with phase-dependent observations. A useful minimal species model is limiting reagent R converting through competing pathways to target P and impurity/byproduct B:

R → P,  R → B, and possibly P → degradation products.

For catalyst c, solvent s, and temperature T, a tentative kinetic representation is

dR/dt = −k(c,s,T)R,

dP/dt = φ(c,s,T)kR − kd(c,s,T)P,

where k controls conversion, φ is target-forming selectivity, and kd represents target degradation. An Arrhenius-like temperature dependence, k = A(c,s)exp(−Ea(c,s)/RT), is plausible, but the campaign cannot identify A or Ea because temperature and duration were changed together. Catalyst and solvent are anonymous categories; their indices have no chemical ordering.

## Reaction evidence

Batches 2–7 formed the initial short-condition screen at 350 K for 1200 s, using 0.040 mol reagent, 0.050 L solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, and 700 rpm. All gave low final conversion:

- Batch 2, C0/S1: conversion 0.098, purity 0.427, recovery 0.043, selectivity 0.411.
- Batch 3, C0/S2: conversion 0.108, purity 0.488, recovery 0.062, selectivity 0.478.
- Batch 4, C0/S3: conversion 0.131, purity 0.326, recovery 0.038, selectivity 0.313.
- Batch 5, C1/S0: conversion 0.084, purity 0.526, recovery 0.046, selectivity 0.523.
- Batch 6, C2/S0: conversion 0.090, purity 0.215, recovery 0.021, selectivity 0.202.
- Batch 7, C3/S0: conversion 0.079, purity 0.404, recovery 0.032, selectivity 0.392.

These observations suggested that short residence time was limiting overall conversion, while catalyst and solvent mainly changed pathway selectivity. Within the tested short C1–C3/S0 comparison, C1 was most target-selective and C2 least selective. Within C0/S1–S3, S2 was numerically best. Because each condition was run only once, small differences should not be interpreted as precisely resolved effects.

Batch 8 changed the explanation substantially. C1/S0 at 400 K for 7200 s gave conversion 0.721, purity 0.534, recovery 0.335, and selectivity 0.493. Compared with batch 5 at 350 K and 1200 s, conversion rose from 0.084 to 0.721 while selectivity remained near 0.5. Thus temperature and/or residence time strongly controls extent of reaction, whereas this change did not greatly improve the intrinsic product/byproduct split. The design confounds temperature with time, so it cannot determine which variable caused how much of the increase.

Batches 8–11 then compared solvents under the common long condition C1, 400 K, 7200 s:

- Batch 8, S0: conversion 0.721, purity 0.534, recovery 0.335, selectivity 0.493.
- Batch 9, S1: conversion 0.759, purity 0.526, recovery 0.369, selectivity 0.472.
- Batch 10, S2: conversion 0.836, purity 0.576, recovery 0.432, selectivity 0.512.
- Batch 11, S3: conversion 0.788, purity 0.353, recovery 0.232, selectivity 0.300.

This supports a catalyst–solvent coupling rather than a purely kinetic solvent effect. S2 gave the best observed balance with C1, while S3 allowed substantial conversion but diverted much more material toward impurity/byproduct. In the simple model, S2 increases k and/or reduces target degradation relative to S0/S1, whereas S3 chiefly lowers φ. Batch 10 was therefore the strongest unpurified reaction result, although its purity of 0.576 remained far below the required 0.80.

Long reactions also produced larger byproduct signals: batch 10 had byproduct signal 0.329 and degradation warning 0.043. This is consistent with competing product formation and degradation accumulating as conversion rises, but those two processes are not separately identifiable.

## Extraction and purification

The nominal dossier for X0 reported Kproduct = 1.477, Kimpurity = 0.635 and selectivity ratio S* = 2.328 under a 0.030 L aqueous/0.018 L organic contact at 298.15 K. It predicted organic fractions of approximately 0.410 for product and 0.241 for impurity. If those constants transferred directly, extraction would multiply the product-to-impurity odds by roughly 2.33, improving purity at the cost of retaining only about 41% of product in one organic contact.

Actual process evidence did not support direct transfer of that dossier model.

Batch 1 used C0/S0 at 350 K for 1200 s, followed by 0.030 L aqueous phase, 0.018 L X0, mixing for 240 s at 700 rpm, settling, organic-phase selection, a 0.020 L wash, drying, and concentration. Before workup, HPLC showed conversion 0.091, purity 0.395, recovery 0.052, and yield 0.035. The final organic material showed purity 0.742 but measured recovery 0, yield 0.007, and selectivity 0.011. Thus workup appeared to enrich a very small residual target signal but lost essentially all recoverable target.

Batch 12 tested the same extraction concept on the much better C1/S2 long-reaction feed. Before extraction, HPLC measured conversion 0.808, purity 0.578, recovery 0.421, selectivity 0.535, and yield 0.435. After adding 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.018 L X0, mixing, settling, retaining the organic phase, washing with 0.040 L, and drying, the final assay gave purity 0.325 and recovery 0.038. Only about 9% of the pre-workup recovery remained. The final phase-specific conversion was 0.999, but this must not be read as global reaction conversion: unreacted reagent can preferentially remain in a discarded phase, making conversion in the retained phase appear nearly complete.

Batch 12 therefore falsified my initial operational assumption that the X0 dossier would predict this reaction mixture. Plausible explanations include matrix-dependent partitioning, dossier misindexing (explicitly allowed by the material information), interaction with reaction solvent S2, loss of target during washing, or a mismatch between the dossier’s simple product/impurity anchors and the multicomponent reaction mixture. Batch 1 and batch 12 also differed in wash volume, feed composition, and concentration step, so the exact loss mechanism cannot be isolated.

## Measurement and phase coupling

Reaction metrics and downstream metrics are not interchangeable assays of the same material. Before separation they describe the reactor liquid; after phase selection they describe only the retained phase. Consequently:

- Apparent conversion can increase because reactant partitions away, not because additional reaction occurred.
- Purity can increase while absolute recovery collapses, as in batch 1.
- A final phase can show near-unit conversion but very low target yield and selectivity, as in batches 1 and 12.

For process evaluation, recovery relative to the original 0.040 mol charge is therefore the essential extensive metric, while purity is an intensive composition metric. Both must be considered together.

## Scope and unresolved factors

The conclusions apply only to the tested fixed reagent, catalyst loading, solvent volume, stirring rate, and anonymous material categories. Important unresolved factors include:

1. Temperature versus time: 350 K/1200 s and 400 K/7200 s were compared, so their effects are confounded.
2. Catalyst loading: all substantive runs used 0.005 mol; no rate or selectivity dependence on loading was measured.
3. Replication: every recipe was run once, so fine rankings lack repeatability estimates beyond declared instrument noise.
4. Catalyst–solvent interactions: only C0 across several solvents at short conditions and C1 across several solvents at long conditions were explored; most of the 4×4 categorical space remains unmeasured.
5. Degradation kinetics: degradation warning and byproduct signal were observed, but formation and destruction pathways were not separately resolved.
6. Extraction identity: only X0 was experimentally used; X1–X3 were not tested despite the possibility that the dossier was unreliable or misindexed.
7. Workup operations: extraction, phase selection, washing, drying, and—in batch 1—concentration were bundled, preventing attribution of losses to one operation.
8. Phase equilibrium: only one contact ratio and mixing/settling schedule was tested. Equilibrium attainment and entrainment were not independently verified.
9. Atmosphere, pressure, headspace, and controlled ramps were not varied.

## Plausible alternative models

An alternative to simple parallel first-order kinetics is a solvent-controlled intermediate network, R ⇌ I → P or B, in which solvent changes intermediate stabilization and long residence drives different branches. Another possibility is catalyst deactivation: C1 may retain activity under long heating better than other catalysts, making its apparent advantage kinetic rather than intrinsically selective. The data cannot distinguish these from the minimal parallel-pathway model.

For workup, a multicomponent partition model is more plausible than constant two-solute distribution coefficients. One could write, for each species i,

ni,org / ni,aq = Ki(X,T,solvent composition,pH,loading),

with Ki changing after reaction solvent carryover and washing. The campaign identifies neither these functions nor pH effects.

## Overall conclusion

The best-supported reaction recipe was batch 10: C1/S2, 400 K, 7200 s, 700 rpm, which produced recovery 0.432 and purity 0.576 before any successful purification. Higher temperature/longer time increased conversion dramatically, while catalyst–solvent identity controlled the target/byproduct split. The attempted X0 extraction workflow was the dominant failure: it sharply reduced recovery and did not reproducibly increase purity. No completed batch met purity ≥0.80. Batch 1, the sealed recommendation, was selected only because its final purity of 0.742 was closest to the hard constraint; its zero measured recovery means it is not a feasible successful process. The most informative next study, if a new campaign were allowed, would be a phase-retention and extractant screen on the C1/S2 long-reaction feed, with assays before and after each individual workup operation.

payload.rationale: The main extrapolation anchor is campaign batch 10 (C1/S2, 400 K, 7200 s), which reached pre-workup/final recovery about 0.43 and purity about 0.58 at 0.005 mol catalyst per 0.040 mol reagent. Q01–Q06 use twentyfold lower catalyst-to-reagent ratio, so I expect low conversion and very small final recovery, with 7200 s outperforming 1800 s. Their intervals are especially wide because catalyst-loading dependence was never measured. For X2, the dossier implies only moderate product-over-impurity partition selectivity; larger organic volume should increase recovery more than purity. X0 receives a lower and much less certain purity prediction because the two observed X0 workups, especially batch 12, contradicted its nominal dossier and caused severe target loss. Q07–Q12 restore the catalyst-to-reagent ratio used in the campaign, so their recovery estimates are materially higher despite dilution. Washing is predicted to raise purity while sacrificing target recovery, with two staged washes giving a modest additional purity gain and loss relative to one equal-total wash. Concentration should mostly remove solvent, so Q11 and Q12 are predicted to be similar, with a small possible recovery penalty after concentration. The broad 80% intervals reflect unmeasured catalyst-loading and dilution laws, lack of replication, uncertain X2 matrix transfer, and bundled extraction, washing, drying, concentration, and transfer losses.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No separate instance-specific prior, hidden optimum, or required mechanistic law was supplied. The only substantive supplied prior was the nominal extractant dossier, explicitly described as incomplete and potentially misindexed.

Supported within the tested scope:
- Reaction extent depends strongly on temperature and/or residence time. C1/S0 gave conversion 0.084 in batch 5 at 350 K for 1200 s, versus 0.721 in batch 8 at 400 K for 7200 s. This changed my judgment from primarily screening material identity to treating reaction severity as a major limiting variable. Temperature and time remain confounded.
- Catalyst and solvent affect pathway selectivity, not merely rate. In the short S0 comparison, final selectivity was 0.523 for C1 in batch 5, 0.202 for C2 in batch 6, and 0.392 for C3 in batch 7. Under the long C1 condition, S2 in batch 10 gave purity/recovery 0.576/0.432, while S3 in batch 11 gave 0.353/0.232 despite substantial conversion. This supports categorical catalyst–solvent coupling.
- Phase-specific conversion is not global reaction conversion. Batch 12 moved from pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.808 to final conversion 0.999 while recovery fell from 0.421 to 0.038. Phase disposal, rather than further reaction, explains that apparent conversion increase.

Contradicted or not operationally transferable:
- The initial working claim that X0 would be a favorable organic extractor was contradicted. Batch 1 ended at purity 0.742 but zero measured recovery. More decisively, batch 12 changed from pre-workup purity/recovery 0.578/0.421 to final 0.325/0.038 after the X0 workflow. Thus the dossier constants did not predict the complete reaction-mixture workup.
- The implicit expectation that extraction plus washing would solve the purity constraint was contradicted: no batch achieved purity at least 0.80.

Untested or underidentified:
- An Arrhenius law, individual temperature and time effects, reaction order, catalyst-loading dependence, catalyst deactivation, and target-degradation kinetics were not identified.
- X1, X2, and X3 were never experimentally tested during the campaign. Consequently, the later predictions involving X2 were extrapolations from its nominal dossier rather than campaign validation.
- Most catalyst–solvent combinations, phase ratios, staged washes, dilution effects, and atmosphere/pressure effects remained untested.
- Every recipe lacked replication, so small numerical rankings cannot establish repeatable effects.

2. One discriminating experiment

I would repeat the batch-10 reaction feed—C1/S2 at 400 K for 7200 s—and apply the batch-12 X0 extraction, but obtain stage-resolved HPLC measurements of the selected organic phase immediately after separation and again after the wash/dry step, using minimal samples. The final assay would still be performed on the finished organic material.

My leading explanation is that the dossier partition behavior fails in the actual reaction matrix or is misindexed. The main alternative is that initial partitioning is acceptable but washing, drying, or associated handling causes most of the target loss.

- If the organic phase is already target-poor immediately after separation, especially with low recovery and no purity enrichment, I would strengthen the matrix-dependent/misindexed-partition explanation.
- If the first organic measurement shows the expected enrichment and substantial recovery but the post-wash measurement collapses, I would instead attribute the failure chiefly to washing or later handling.
- If both intermediate measurements retain target but the final assay is poor, concentration, transfer, termination, or an assay-domain issue would become the leading alternative.
- If the repeated process performs well throughout, I would reduce confidence in both explanations and treat batch 12 as evidence of large process variability, making replication essential.

3. Unused evidence and reliability

Unused evidence included the raw public spectral artifacts: I relied on processed HPLC and final-assay estimates and did not inspect the detailed chromatograms or spectra. I also did not use GC, NMR, IR, MS, or UV–visible measurements; assay both discarded and retained phases; measure a reaction time course; test X1–X3; or replicate any recipe. The nominal X1–X3 dossier entries therefore remained unused experimentally. Operational variables such as atmosphere, pressure, headspace, ramp rate, and catalyst loading were also left unexplored.

The least reliable predictions are Q01–Q06 because they extrapolate to a catalyst-to-reagent ratio twentyfold below the campaign value without an observed loading law. All X2 predictions are weak because X2 was never tested, and the failure of the X0 dossier warns that nominal partition constants may not transfer to reaction mixtures. Q07–Q12 additionally extrapolate to a much smaller reagent charge and different dilution. Predictions about staged washing and concentration are particularly uncertain because those effects were bundled rather than independently measured.

The sealed batch-1 recommendation is not a reliable successful operating recommendation: it was chosen only as the closest observed approach to the hard purity constraint, with purity 0.742, while its measured recovery was zero. Batch 10 is the more reliable reaction-stage recommendation, but it is not a complete feasible process because purity was only 0.576.

The assigned goal affected evidence collection. The hard purity requirement encouraged completion of extraction and purification workflows and ultimately drove selection toward the highest-purity batch rather than the highest-recovery batch. At the same time, early resources were spent screening reaction categories and severity, leaving only two X0 workups and no genuine extractant screen. Using one HPLC observation per batch gave useful reaction-stage evidence but insufficient stage-by-stage mass-balance evidence. This was a design tradeoff rather than evidence of a conflict in the observations.

recommendation.selection_rationale: No completed batch met purity >=0.80. Batch 1 is the closest constraint approach (final purity 0.742) and is therefore selected over the higher-recovery but much less pure batch 10. Its measured recovery was 0, so this is explicitly a constraint-proximity recommendation rather than a successful feasible process; the campaign indicates separation chemistry must be re-screened.
